analysis.one_liner: Directs the EPA to ban all manufacture, import, and use of asbestos.
analysis.headline: The asbestos ban bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the nation's main toxic-chemicals law to require the Environmental Protection Agency to identify how asbestos is imported, sold, and used, then impose rules that permanently eliminate any chance of people or the environment being exposed to it. The ban would generally take effect within about two years, with a narrow exemption the President could grant for national-security uses where no alternative exists.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who might be exposed to asbestos, including workers in industries that handle it and residents of buildings containing asbestos products. Asbestos is a known carcinogen linked to mesothelioma and other fatal diseases, so eliminating exposure reduces future cancer cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and residents exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: The bill required the EPA to publish an assessment of current and anticipated asbestos importation, distribution, uses, and exposures within 90 days of enactment.

Within 18 months, the EPA had to impose prohibitions on the manufacture, processing, use, distribution in commerce, and disposal of asbestos and asbestos-containing articles, chosen so as to permanently eliminate the possibility of exposure.

The only exception was a Presidential exemption, capped at three years per grant, for uses the President finds necessary to national security, with no reasonable alternative and no unreasonable health or environmental risk.

analysis.who_pays: Importers of asbestos and manufacturers and users of asbestos-containing products, such as some industrial and chemical-processing operations, would have to stop using asbestos and find substitutes. Some of those compliance costs could be passed to consumers.

drawbacks.text: A near-total ban within roughly two years would have forced rapid changes for industrial processes that still used asbestos, and the costs of compliance could raise prices for products where no substitute was readily available.

The bill's own structure acknowledged hard cases: it let the President exempt national-security-related uses for up to three years at a time, which critics could note kept some exposure pathways open.
The one-size mandate gave the EPA little room to weigh costs against the stringency of the rules; the exemption standard explicitly bars consideration of costs or other non-risk factors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit of eliminating human exposure to a known carcinogen is large and permanent, while the costs fall on a relatively small set of industrial users who would need substitutes. The main design criticism is the speed and rigidity of the mandate, which could have caused disruption where workable alternatives are scarce, though the national-security exemption offered a narrow safety valve.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice in the Senate and sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, and it stayed there without any hearing, markup, or vote until the 114th Congress ended in early January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer of California introduced the bill in the Senate on September 28, 2016, joined by Senator Jon Tester of Montana.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

The bill was introduced less than three months before the end of a two-year Congress, after the summer 2016 enactment of the broader Toxic Substances Control Act overhaul, which revised chemical-safety procedures without imposing an outright asbestos ban.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Importers and industrial users of asbestos, who kept operating under existing rules, remained better off because the bill never advanced; future exposures to asbestos that the bill would have eliminated continued.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.role: U.S. Senator from California; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it was introduced 'for herself and Mr. Tester.'

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired in the 114th Congress by Sen. Jim Inhofe (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and took no action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats; the bill had only two supporters in the Senate and no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-chaired committee it was referred to never acted on it.

industries.industry: Asbestos importers and manufacturers of asbestos-containing products
industries.note: The bill would have banned the manufacture, import, and use of asbestos and asbestos-containing articles within about two years, ending these companies' product lines. Their continued revenue depends on a material the bill treats as a carcinogen that must be eliminated.
Producers of replacement materials for asbestos-containing uses, such as alternative industrial components, stood to gain customers from a mandated phaseout.
